--- title: "Sequential Decisions and Dynamic Programming" subtitle: "Lecture 20" author: "Vivek Srikrishnan" course: "BEE 4750" institution: "Cornell University" date: "November 18, 2026" format: revealjs: slide-number: c/t show-slide-number: all center-title-slide: true width: 1280 height: 720 transition: none toc: true toc-depth: 1 toc-title: "Overview" history: false link-external-newwindow: true theme: ../sass/slides.scss template-partials: - title-slide.html menu: numbers: true html-math-method: mathjax include-in-header: mathjax-config.html date-format: long email-obfuscation: javascript chalkboard: theme: whiteboard buttons: true controls: true engine: julia julia: exeflags: ["+1.11.5"] execute: freeze: auto daemon: 600 --- # Review of Last Class ## Scenario Trees Grow Fast - Two-stage problems: **one** here-and-now decision, **one recourse decision per scenario**. - With a decision **every** period and uncertainty **every** period, the tree branches again each time: 3 outcomes a year for 10 years is 59,049 leaves. Today: decisions in a **sequence**, and a way to solve them without writing out the tree. ::: {.notes} Two minutes. Monday's farmer made one decision, learned the yield, and adjusted. Most environmental decisions repeat: release water every month, set a loading every year, harvest every season. Writing out every path through the future quickly becomes impossible. Dynamic programming is the standard way around it. ::: ## Questions? :::: {.columns .center} ::: {.column width="40%"} ![](figures/vsrikrish-poll.png){fig-alt="Poll Everywhere QR Code" fig-align="center" width="100%"} ::: ::: {.column width=60%} **Text**: VSRIKRISH to 22333 **URL**: [https://pollev.com/vsrikrish](https://pollev.com/vsrikrish)

[See Results](https://www.polleverywhere.com/multiple_choice_polls/qKeig0hHShZYHAOmvZtZm?preview=true&controls=none){preview-link="true"} ::: :::: # Sequential Decisions ## Decisions Linked Over Time - **Reservoir**: water released this month is not there next month. - **Lake** (week 3): $P_{t+1} = P_t + L_t - sP_t + R(P_t)$. This year's loading $L_t$ sets next year's lake. - **Fishery**: this season's harvest sets next season's stock. **Why not just optimize each month on its own?** ::: {.notes} About five minutes. Each example has a stock that carries the past into the future, so today's decision changes tomorrow's options. The lake equation is the one from week 3: students have already seen a state that evolves from year to year; today the loading becomes a decision. Pose the question and take answers; the reservoir example answers it. ::: ## A Reservoir in a Dry Season - Storage holds up to **4 units**, and starts **full**. - Each month: **release** $r$ (at most what is stored), then the month's **inflow** arrives; anything above 4 spills. - Inflows over the season: 1, 1, 0. - Benefit of a month's release: | Release | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | |:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:| | **Benefit** | 0 | 6 | 10 | 12 | 13 | ::: {.notes} About three minutes. Small numbers on purpose: everything today can be done by hand. The benefits have diminishing returns: the first unit released in a month is worth 6, the second only 4 more, the third 2, the fourth 1. Think of water for irrigation or a city during a dry season. ::: ## The Greedy Plan **Greedy**: release everything available, every month. It releases 4, 1, 1, for a total benefit of **25**. **Can you beat 25?** ::: {.fragment .fade-in} Releasing 2, 2, 2 gives a total of **30**. Spreading the water out wins, because the second unit in a month is worth less than the first unit in another month. ::: ::: {.notes} About four minutes, with a poll or a minute of pair work. Greedy maximizes each month's benefit separately: it empties the reservoir in month 1, then only has the inflow. Most students find 2, 2, 2 quickly. The harder question is how to find the best plan when there are more months, more storage levels, or uncertain inflows: trial and error does not scale. ::: ## The Ingredients - **Stage** $t$: the month. - **State** $s_t$: storage at the start of the month; it carries the past forward. - **Decision** $r_t$: the release, with $0 \leq r_t \leq s_t$. - **Transition**: $s_{t+1} = \min(s_t - r_t + I_t,\ 4)$. - **Value function** $V_t(s)$: the best total benefit from month $t$ to the end, starting with storage $s$. - **Policy**: the best release for each month and storage level. ::: {.notes} About four minutes. These names are the vocabulary for the rest of the lecture and for Monday's lab. The value function is the key idea: it answers "how good is it to be here?" for every state, not only the one we start in. Once we know next month's value function, choosing this month's release is a one-step problem. ::: # Backward Induction ## Start at the End In the **last month**, nothing comes after, so release everything: | Storage | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | |:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:| | **Best release** | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | | **Value** $V_3(s)$ | 0 | 6 | 10 | 12 | 13 | Now step **backwards**: knowing $V_3$, month 2 is a one-step problem. ::: {.notes} About two minutes. The last stage is the easy one, because there is no future to protect. That is why we start there. ::: ## Month 2, by Hand For each storage $s$, try every release $r \leq s$ (month 2's inflow is $I_2 =$ 1): $$V_2(s) = \max_{r \leq s} \left[\, \text{benefit}(r) + V_3\big(\min(s - r + I_2,\ 4)\big) \right]$$ **Your turn: compute $V_2(3)$.** ::: {.fragment .fade-in} | Storage | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | |:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:| | **Best release** | 0 | 1 | 1 | 2 | 2 | | **Value** $V_2(s)$ | 6 | 12 | 16 | 20 | 22 | ::: ::: {.notes} Board item, about ten minutes. Work V2(0) and V2(1) together on the board, then let students compute V2(3). For s = 3 the options are: release 0, benefit 0 plus V3 of min(3 + 1, 4) = 13, so 13; release 1, 6 plus V3(3) = 12, so 18; release 2, 10 plus V3(2) = 10, so 20; release 3, 12 plus V3(1) = 6, so 18. The best is 20, releasing 2. Fill in the rest of the table. At storage 2 and storage 4 two releases tie (1 or 2, and 2 or 3); the table reports the smaller one. ::: ## Backward Induction in Code ::: {#14 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="false"} function backward_induction(inflow; end_value=zeros(capacity + 1)) value = fill(-Inf, capacity + 1, n_months + 1) # best total from month t policy = zeros(Int, capacity + 1, n_months) # best release value[:, n_months + 1] = end_value # water left at the end for t in n_months:-1:1, s in levels for r in 0:s # at most what is stored total = benefit(r) + value[next_storage(s, r, inflow[t]) + 1, t + 1] if total > value[s + 1, t] # ties keep the smaller r value[s + 1, t] = total policy[s + 1, t] = r end end end return value, policy end ``` ::: ::: {.notes} About four minutes. The code is the hand calculation in a loop: months backwards, every storage level, every allowed release (no more than is stored). It keeps one table of values and one table of best releases, both allocated at full size before the loop. A release replaces the best so far only if it is strictly better, so ties keep the smaller release, as on the board. ::: ## Month 1, and the Plan | Storage | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | |:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:| | **Best release** | 0 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 2 | | **Value** $V_1(s)$ | 12 | 18 | 22 | 26 | 30 | From a full reservoir, $V_1(4) =$ **30**. Following the policy forward gives releases **2, 2, 2**. ::: {.notes} About three minutes. The value function at the start answers the whole problem: 30, against greedy's 25. To get the plan, follow the policy forward: release 2, see the storage, look up the next month's best release, and so on. ::: ## Checking by Brute Force ::: {#20 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true"} # Try every release sequence (only feasible because the problem is tiny) function brute_force() best_total = -1 n_best = 0 # how many sequences reach the best total for r1 in 0:start_storage s2 = next_storage(start_storage, r1, inflow[1]) for r2 in 0:s2 s3 = next_storage(s2, r2, inflow[2]) for r3 in 0:s3 total = benefit(r1) + benefit(r2) + benefit(r3) if total > best_total best_total = total n_best = 1 elseif total == best_total n_best += 1 end end end end return best_total, n_best end best_total, n_best = brute_force() ``` ::: Checking every release sequence directly, the best total is **30**, and **1** sequence reaches it. Backward induction found it. ::: {.notes} About two minutes. Verification as a named step: on a problem this small we can try every sequence and confirm the answer. On a realistic problem we cannot, which is exactly why we need a method we have checked on cases where we can. ::: ## Why Spread the Water? ::: {#cell-fig-releases .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true"} months = 1:n_months p_releases = bar(months .- 0.18, greedy_release, bar_width=0.35, color=cb_vermillion, linecolor=:black, label="Greedy (total $(greedy_total))", xlabel="Month", ylabel="Release [units]", legend=:topright, ylims=(0, 5), xticks=months) bar!(p_releases, months .+ 0.18, dp_release, bar_width=0.35, color=cb_blue, linecolor=:black, fillstyle=:/, label="DP (total $(dp_total))") plot!(p_releases, size=(1050, 330), left_margin=10mm, bottom_margin=10mm) ``` ::: {#fig-releases .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` Monthly releases under the greedy plan and the dynamic programming plan. ::: ::: With diminishing returns, the best plan **equalizes** the releases. ::: {.notes} About three minutes. Interpretation after the result. With diminishing returns, moving a unit from a month with a big release to a month with a small one always gains, until the releases are equal. Greedy ignores that the water could have been used later. ::: # Uncertain Inflows ## Releasing Before the Inflow Is Known Inflow is **0 or 2 units**, equally likely, and is unknown when we release, so we use the **expected** next value: $$ \begin{aligned} V_t(s) = \max_{r \leq s} \Big[\, \text{benefit}(r) &+ \tfrac{1}{2} V_{t+1}\big(\min(s - r, 4)\big) \\ &+ \tfrac{1}{2} V_{t+1}\big(\min(s - r + 2, 4)\big) \Big] \end{aligned} $$ The backward pass is the same, and the answer is a **policy**: the best release for each storage level. ::: {.notes} About three minutes. The only change from the deterministic case is that the next storage depends on an inflow we do not know yet, so we average the next month's value over the two possibilities. Because we cannot know the future storage, the useful answer is a rule: what to release for any storage we might find ourselves in. ::: ## Hedging ::: {#24 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true"} inflow_outcomes = [0, 2] inflow_probs = [0.5, 0.5] function backward_induction_uncertain(n_periods) value = fill(-Inf, capacity + 1, n_periods + 1) value[:, n_periods + 1] .= 0 policy = zeros(Int, capacity + 1, n_periods) for t in n_periods:-1:1 for s in levels for r in 0:s # average next month's value over the possible inflows expected_next = 0.0 for k in eachindex(inflow_outcomes) next_s = next_storage(s, r, inflow_outcomes[k]) expected_next = expected_next + inflow_probs[k] * value[next_s + 1, t + 1] end total = benefit(r) + expected_next if total > value[s + 1, t] value[s + 1, t] = total policy[s + 1, t] = r end end end end return value, policy end value_u, policy_u = backward_induction_uncertain(n_months) # Expected benefit of releasing everything every month, from storage s in month t function release_all_expected(s, t) if t > n_months return 0.0 end expected_next = 0.0 for k in eachindex(inflow_outcomes) next_s = next_storage(s, s, inflow_outcomes[k]) expected_next = expected_next + inflow_probs[k] * release_all_expected(next_s, t + 1) end return benefit(s) + expected_next end release_all_value = release_all_expected(start_storage, 1) ``` ::: From a full reservoir the policy releases **2** and holds 2 in case it doesn't rain. Its expected benefit is **28\.25**; releasing everything gets 23. ::: {.notes} About four minutes. Even though the reservoir is full and rain might come, the policy releases only 2 in the first month: holding water is insurance against a dry month. That is hedging. Releasing everything immediately does much worse in expectation. If asked, the full policy table is in the value_u and policy_u arrays; at low storage the policy releases less. ::: ## Check It Against the Scenario Tree ::: {#26 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true"} # Monday's method: a decision at every node of the tree, then the best # expected value, by brute-force recursion over all branches function tree_value(s, t) if t > n_months return 0.0 end best = -Inf for r in 0:s expected = 0.0 for k in eachindex(inflow_outcomes) next_s = next_storage(s, r, inflow_outcomes[k]) expected = expected + inflow_probs[k] * tree_value(next_s, t + 1) end best = max(best, benefit(r) + expected) end return best end tree_best = tree_value(start_storage, 1) ``` ::: Enumerating every branch of the scenario tree gives **28\.25**, and dynamic programming gives the same **28\.25**. ::: {.notes} About two minutes. Verification against Monday's method. The tree allows a different decision at every node; dynamic programming gets the same optimum because the best decision at a node depends only on the storage there, not on how we got there. That property is what lets the table replace the tree. ::: ## Trees Versus Tables | Months | Tree leaves | DP table entries | |:--|--:|--:| | 3 | 8 | 15 | | 6 | 64 | 30 | | 12 | 4,096 | 60 | With 2 inflow outcomes a month and 5 storage levels, the tree grows **exponentially** with the number of months; the table grows **linearly**. ::: {.notes} About three minutes. The tree records every possible history; the table records only the states that matter for the future. That is the whole trick of dynamic programming. The catch, in the appendix, is that the table grows exponentially with the number of state variables instead: the curse of dimensionality. ::: ## What Is Water Worth at the End? ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true"} carryover_values = [0, 3, 6] # value of each unit left in storage at the end println("| Value per unit left at the end | Releases | Storage left |") println("|:--|:--|--:|") for c in carryover_values v, pol = backward_induction(inflow; end_value=c .* levels) rel = zeros(Int, n_months) s = start_storage for t in 1:n_months rel[t] = pol[s + 1, t] s = next_storage(s, rel[t], inflow[t]) end println("| ", c, " | ", join(rel, ", "), " | ", s, " |") end ``` | Value per unit left at the end | Releases | Storage left | |:--|:--|--:| | 0 | 2, 2, 2 | 0 | | 3 | 2, 2, 2 | 0 | | 6 | 1, 1, 0 | 4 | The **end-of-horizon value** is a modelling choice that can flip the plan: what is water worth in October? ::: {.notes} About four minutes. With no value on leftover water, the plan empties the reservoir by the end of the season. Value leftover water at 6 per unit and the plan holds most of it back. Neither is wrong: it depends on whether the reservoir refills in winter. The default today, zero, assumes it does. This is the dynamic programming version of the horizon problem we will see again in the limits-of-optimization lecture. ::: # Key Takeaways ## Key Takeaways - A **sequential decision** has stages, a **state** that carries the past forward, and a **transition**; deciding each month on its own (greedy) can be badly wrong (25 vs. 30). - **Backward induction**: start at the end, keep one **value function** per stage, step backwards. - Under uncertainty, DP returns a **policy** and matches the scenario tree's answer, with a table that grows linearly instead of exponentially. - **Trap**: the end-of-horizon value can flip the plan. ::: {.notes} About two minutes. ::: # Upcoming Schedule ## Next Classes **Monday, November 23**: Lab 4, scenario trees and sequential decisions for reservoir operations. It builds on today's model (bring a laptop). **Wednesday, November 25**: No class (Thanksgiving). **Monday, November 30**: Multiple objectives, robustness, and sensitivity. ## Assessments **HW8** and **MP2**: due Thursday, November 19. **Quiz 6**: Monday, December 7. # Appendix ## The Bellman Recursion In general notation, with state $s$, decision $r$, benefit $b$, and random inflow $q$: $$V_t(s) = \max_{r} \left\{ b(r) + \mathbb{E}_q\left[V_{t+1}\big(f(s, r, q)\big)\right] \right\}$$ $$V_{T+1}(s) = \text{terminal value}$$ where $f$ is the transition. Everything in the lecture is this equation with small numbers. ## The Curse of Dimensionality | Reservoirs | Storage states (5 levels each) | |:--|--:| | 1 | 5 | | 2 | 25 | | 10 | 9,765,625 | The table is small for one state variable, but it grows exponentially with the **number** of state variables. Dynamic programming avoids the tree's growth over time, but its table grows exponentially with the number of state variables instead. ## Does the Storage Grid Matter? ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true"} # Finer storage grids, with the benefit interpolated linearly between table points function benefit_interp(r) if r >= capacity return Float64(benefit_table[end]) end k = floor(Int, r) fraction = r - k return (1 - fraction) * benefit_table[k + 1] + fraction * benefit_table[k + 2] end function best_from_full(spacing) grid = 0:spacing:capacity n = length(grid) value = zeros(n, n_months + 1) for t in n_months:-1:1 for i in 1:n s = grid[i] best = -Inf for r in 0:spacing:s j = round(Int, min(s - r + inflow[t], capacity) / spacing) + 1 best = max(best, benefit_interp(r) + value[j, t + 1]) end value[i, t] = best end end return value[end, 1] end println("| Grid spacing (units) | Best total from a full reservoir |") println("|:--|--:|") for spacing in [1, 0.5, 0.25] println("| ", fmt(spacing), " | ", fmt(best_from_full(spacing)), " |") end ``` | Grid spacing (units) | Best total from a full reservoir | |:--|--:| | 1 | 30 | | 0.5 | 30 | | 0.25 | 30 | The answer does not change as the storage grid is refined. ## The Lake as a Dynamic Program - **State**: phosphorus $P_t$ in the lake. - **Decision**: loading $L_t$ each year. - **Transition**: $P_{t+1} = P_t + L_t - sP_t + R(P_t)$ (week 3). - **Benefit**: the value of the loading (farm output, wastewater), minus damages when the lake is eutrophic. A continuous state with a threshold needs a fine grid in $P$.
